newsitem.title: UK: Minor metals - Sluggish, drifting in summer lull.
newsitem.headline: Minor metals - Sluggish, drifting in summer lull.

text.p: Minor metals lacked feature over the past week as consumers and market players held the sidelines in slow summer conditions.
Antimony drifted lower, while recent star performer bismuth eased under Chinese offers. Elsewhere, prices held tight ranges and were showing few signs of breaking out.
"Quiet is being upbeat," one relaxed trader said.
Antimony moved lower to straddle the $2,000 level on flurries of offers from China, though little business was concluded.
Antimony like the rest of the sector is drifting lower amid the lack of interest, prices look set to decline further," one trader commented.
Traders noted news that January-May exports of unwrought antimony reached 14,695 tonnes, up 33.6 percent compared with year-ago period.

Chinese offers after a recent spike to around $4.00 a pound took the heat out of bismuth. Offers were seen around $3.50 down $3.40, traders said "It's off the boil and set to head further south," one said.

Cobalt held steady levels. Traders noted news that the Defense National Stockpile Center said the U.S. Court of Federal Claims had lifted its injunction on sealed bid cobalt sales following a legal dispute with Minor Metals. This levels the way open to a resumption of offers to the market. Stockpile has the right to offer all the cobalt is has left in the little time remaining in its current fiscal year to September 30, but it was unlikely to do so.
So far the news has failed to impact on the market, though it could apply downside pressure medium-term.
Russian supply was said to be thin on the ground due to floods at Dudinka. Traders said shipments from Russia would not arrive in Europe until end-July/early-August.

Magnesium was a hard market to pin down. Several traders said the market was tight, while others said Russian stockpiled material was available. However, traders said that the stockpiled material was unlikely to hit the Western spot market as domestic producers are lobbying hard for the surplus metal.
One downside trader said that a merchant had offered at around $2,348 a tonne for Chinese material at an Egyptian tender.
This could put downside pressure on the market.
Chinese offers and lower producer prices put pressure on indium, while rhodium continued to ease after chasing sister platinum group metal palladium higher. --London Newsroom +44 171 542-8075
